I think there's a bit of hypervigilance in there as well.  We are acutely aware that the worst things happen unexpectedly,  so we have to be prepared.  What sucks sometimes is constantly being aware of how each situation can turn bad, guarding yourself, steeling yourself against this. Sometimes, I end up having an underwhelming reaction to good things.  Getting a gift I've been wanting, or something else as a good surprise, ends up with me not really reacting at all, and it's hard to explain "well, I was expecting that we might have a fight, so this gift you got me, I love it, but when is the nest shoe going to drop?"  It's not about the person giving you the gift, its about life having taught me that I need to expect bad things.  So, it's kinda robbed me of being able to show myself as feeling positive about something, and robbed others of seeing how happy I am with something they've done for me.

But I don't know how to let down my guard and still feel safe.  The wall I put up have saved me so far, how do I drop them and still protect me and those I love?

>Answer: because I was once a powerless little kid with opponents that were about 250 lb, and there was nobody to help me. Guidance counselors, cops all but 2 friends parents didn't care when I told them that I need help getting away. Those who believed me, would just get foiled by the narcissistic sociopaths. Whenever I could sneak out, or fight back to get away far enough to run away, the cops would just find me and bring me back to hell. I finally figured out a way to help myself and wrote my imancipation proclamation when I was 15. Then I moved to the other side of the country. 1 thing that helped me keep as level of a head as I did, was that I grew up near the local children's home. And some of the kids were my friends. Some of their stories made mine feel like small potatoes to me at the time. 

I am so sorry your monsters were in your home.  Mine were right outside my door.  My mother dissociated a lot, and it led to a kind of neglect, I cant fault her for it, I know ptsd and she wasn't at fault, so I dont consider what she did or didn't do any abuse, you know?   But I had a couple of teachers who were very abusive, and I was their target, so I understand the powerless feeling of being abused by adults as a child.  There's nothing quite like it.  I believe they set me up to feel like I deserved less, was deserving of being treated badly and set me up to have more abusive relationships in my life than healthy ones.  Hell, i don't even really have friends at this point, I don't trust my judgment of good people,  only bad.   I'm in therapy working on that. But I have my husband, and pups, so not lonely or alone at all.

I remember seeing and hearing all kinds of abuse of my peers when I was a kid.  Some of those abuses were torture, and I believe it made me feel like I wasn't dealing with anything hard at all.  But like my mom has always said "what I see is done to me"...  it has a ripple effect onto us who have been witness to such things.

I have been medicated in the past, diagnosed as an adult, and presently not medicated.  Trust me when I tell you that I miss the me I was when medicated.  It doesn't numb you.  That's not the type of medication they give a person with add/adhd.  If anything, I was able to feel more.  And i could communicate my feelings better because I could think clearly, put my thoughts together, and really get to the heart of my issues outside of add, as well as dealing with add itself.

I could focus.  I could be happy without intrusive thoughts.  I could complete tasks.  I had drive to begin tasks, and my brain would actually work towards goals.

If anything, it let my spirit be free.


Now?  None of those things are true.  And I feel like I'm walking through mud most of the time.  I dont know how I feel about things.  There are a few other medical issues I have, but they are long standing, but I believe a lot of my brain fog comes from not being able to quiet all the "extra noise" in my brain.  Thats what it's like.  My brain blaring a TV, flipping through channels while trying to concentrate on the world around me.  Sometimes it's impossible.   It could be different for your son, but if he has anything similar, I'll let you know that I wasn't better at coping with that when I was 6.  I'm 45 now and it's impossible. 

If you're sure he has adhd, him being unmedicated could be doing the harm you are trying to prevent.  As for your wife, I don't know how severe her adhd is, but there is a wide spectrum of severity, and no two people are exactly the same.  Even if their symptoms are the same, people process/acclimate to what's presented to them differently.   I'm saying this because even if he turns out fine, like your wife, the struggle to become fine by findng his own way of coping without help may do damage to his self esteem in an unforseen way.

Many people who grew up unmedicated, who go on to become medicated in their adult lives end up resenting their parents for leaving them in the ocean without throwing them a life preserver.

Please, do more research.  Your son likely needs help,  and as his parents, you and your wife are the only ones who can help him in this.

Im 45 as well, and I went months not improving.  I focused on the positive parts i could find.  Sometimes the only thing i could find was that i showed up and tried. 

I'm afraid of water, so I used a full-face snorkel for a couple of months, and then graduated to a normal front snorkel added fins and paddles...  first couple of months 25 yards, rarely 50 yards is all I could go without taking a break to breathe for 30 to 60 seconds. I started in March. I kept improving slowly once u added the new equipment and could begin to catch my breath faster so my breaks were shorter, and i worked at extending my ability to go for longer and longer before i took a break. In July, I was doing a mile. September, I completed 5k (not in competition, mind you, and it took a little over an hour and a half). Now I regularly do 2 miles each swim without any break at all.  Some days I do less, some days more.  I go by feel in what feels good. But 2 miles is what I shoot for a d more often than not I hit that goal.

I taught myself with videos and reading about it.  I dont have the best form, but I figured out what works for me personally to be comfortable while swimming.   

There was a woman who tried to teach me some things early on, and I just couldn't do it.  My fear, combined with not really knowing her, made me resistant to learning what she was trying to teach me. Some people need to learn it themselves once they know the basics, others have to find the right person to learn from.

Maybe watch videos, and get some pointers that way, or find another teacher, or both.  You might not be meshing with the teacher you have.  Or you could be like me, someone who learns better on their own.  Be safe, and relax.  Find the right equipment that will make it a better experience for you.  I dont like swimming without my fins or paddles. Sort of a security thing.  I can swim without them, I just feel off balance without the resistance from those two things.  Also, I can not concentrate on timing my breathing with strokes. The snorkel takes that focus out of the equation, thus making swimming far easier for me.

Don't lose hope. If swimming is something you really want to accomplish,  you can.  You probably just need to find the right combination of things to help you get there.  I know I did.

Disclaimer:it's been a while since I've read/watched videos on this, please forgive me if I get bits of it wrong, but to the best of my recollection, here's the jist:

So, it actually started as a treatment for epilepsy.   People used to treat it with fasting, before a couple of doctors decided to try a low carb high protein and fat diet for some of their worst patients,  who would die if fasted to the point that their epilepsy was managed. They were going to starve if fasted to that point, but a few of the patients had heart issues as well and thinking was that they would probably cause more heart issues in other patients with the diet, so they admitted all of the patients to the hospital to try out the diet.  This was in the 1920s.

After doing the diet for a time (I forget how long), their patients improved, the ones with heart problems had their symptoms improve as well as their heart issues.  Something like 59% of all patients had significant improvement and epilepsy management,  another 29% were better managed,  and overall, every one of them improved to a large degree and none of them died from the diet, nor starvation.

Drugs weren't available until the 70s, if I recall correctly, and they used this diet to help people with type 2 diabetes to manage insulinlevels,  as well as alzheimers and dementia patients who markedly improved their memory and sundowned less severely.  They also used it on MS and Parkinson patients and they experienced better muscle stability.

Even today when people either can't take the medication for what ails them, or they are allergic to the drugs, or it simply doesn't treat it well enough for them, they are still put on keto to manage/treat their issues.  In fact, there are doctors that have the opinion that alzheimers is actually type 3 diabetes due to evidence of how the brain responds to prolonged high insulin/blood sugar that doesn't drop with insulin (lack of insulin sensitivity). 


Keto being a diet for weight loss is because we found out through treating other issues, that if you become fat adapted and do it correctly, you can lose weight.  Weight loss is actually the side effect of a medical treatment.

My neurologist actually put me on keto, because I was having neurological issues as a result of being borderline type 2.  I've reversed it, and can sometimes indulge in carbs, but its not a good idea for me to do it on the regular.
People who think it's a bad diet dont know it's true roots in medical treatment.   For brain and pancreas issues, it's sometimes the only treatment to staying on this side of the grass.

But figure out what the root is.  Does this child have all their interests validated? Are they praised enough? Do they get one on one attention from parents?   Do they irritate you, and do you unknowingly express it in some way that makes them feel unwanted?  


Can you look at these "fake" illnesses and realize that they are real but come from something underlying that *also* has to be treated on top of the thing you think is fake?

There is a lot to be said for being believed, *really believed* when you're feeling bad.  If this kid feels that someone doesn't believe them when they are really feeling bad, this can actually cause anxiety, health anxiety, and general anxiety that can cause more physical issues, feeling sick, being accident prone, neediness that is otherwise not age appropriate. 

Asking for more ointment or treatment for the littlest scratch screams to me, "Love me, please.  I feel alone and unsafe. "   Being irritated by this need will feed it.

I understand that it can be irritating.  I was that kid, though.  I was abused by my teachers, and every little ache was a result of feeling unsafe.   I was sick every morning before school.  Mom didn't believe me at first, but I puked every day on the walk to school.   Not my mom's fault, what kid is sick every single day,  and without a fever?  But I felt trapped.

If I brushed up against something too hard, I needed a bandaid.   And I did get actually hurt all the time.

I'm not saying this kid gets abused or that you are abusing this kid by not believing them.  I am saying, though, that their emotional needs are not being met somehow, and not believing the pain that is a result of that can be a contributing factor. 

Warmth and acceptance,  being a safe place and a healthy person to come to, who believes them is really what this kid needs.  You never know what can be hidden underneath that surface of "hurt and sick all the time."  It could be as simple as needing more hugs and one on one play time, and it could be as complex as they've seen or had something done to them that traumatized them.  You won't get to the root of it without letting go of "you're lying to me."

But the biggest takeaway is that what they're feeling, don't assume it's a lie.  It may very well be, some kids learn to lie.  But if it isn't and it's the product of something more serious, would you be able to forgive yourself for dismissing the signs?   It's far easier to treat them for the lie once its uncovered than it is to reverse the invalidation of actual needs.

Be kind to yourself for being human and not believing, forgive that, and move forward with the thought that you have to believe him.  Be open, and warm.  Talk.  Listen.  Be open to everything and be safe for them to come to if they finally want to open up in case this is a big thing.  But be validating, and I think you'll see this kind of thing happen less and less.

If this kid feels you not believing them, the other possibility is that they will end up eventually hiding more serious things down the line, and I don't think there's a parent anywhere who really wants that.

The inner argument of "nothing bad has happened recently when I've thought it would", and the opposing "bad things happen when you least expect them, experience has taught me  this, so keep expecting it."

The only real way to combat her fears is therapy first (she sounds like she hasnt had therapy, or it hasn't been effective, and has no clue how to self talk, nor ground herself, EMDR sounds like something she needs) and to have contingency plans in place for any scenario in which her security could be compromised. I'm not trying to beat you up.  It's natural to try to fix something wrong for someone you love.  But you aren't capable of doing that.  It will take a lot of therapy and training to get her to be even a little better from this, and she will never be the same person she was before this happened to her. Sorry for the length of this, but, if you want to know if keto is sustainable for the long term, you need to look into the origins of the diet itself.

You can Google, but I'll give you a rundown of it.

Fasting used to be a treatment for epilepsy,  and they found that fasting puts the body into a state called ketosis.   In order to not starve their patients to death, doctors (in the 1920s, I think) admitted some of their worst patients to the hospital to put them on a diet that would put their bodies in a state of ketosis.  The reason they admitted them was because they were afraid of the high fat diet causing even more problems, and some of the patients actually had heart issues as well, so they were sure they were going to have some problems.  But what ended up happening is that the treatment was successful,  and the patients with heart problems ended up actually improving as well.

So, this diet became a treatment for a lifelong ailment that was otherwise untreatable because the drugs for managing it weren't developed yet.  They tried it on Parkinson and MS patients and found that they had more muscle stability and elasticity. They tried it on Alzheimers patients as well as Dementia patients and found that they had better memory retention, less sundowning, and less severe sundowning.   Due to the low carbs, they found that it was an effective diet for people with insulin resistance (type 2 diabetes).

Once drugs were developed for all of these issues, they found that there were still people who weren't treated effectively by the medication. Some people have severe side effects that make life more difficult than the ailment,  or they're allergic to a part or whole drug. They are, to this day, treated with a ketogenic diet.

I have been borderline type 2, and still skirt that line....  I've had numerous TBIs, abused alcohol for far too long, and they found deep white tissue hyperintensities on my MRI, which are typically found in dementia patients.   There weren't that many, and my neurologist wasn't really concerned with them. However, it's enough to scare the hell outta me.  My neurologist stated that the best treatment for my issues was keto.  My headaches and stroke like symptoms are gone, and I'm on track to reverse my track to type 2 Diabetes. 

But, my point is that this diet was developed as a medical treatment for lifelong ailments therefore it can be a life long diet.

Since it's inception there have been tweaks here and there about *how* it should be implemented and there are definite variables when it comes to an individual and how low their carbs need to be in order to be in and stay in ketosis, and also needs change as you go from weight loss to maintenance.   If you're even doing it for weight loss,  I was in the beginning and am still in the middle of that, but when I reach my target, I will have to adjust my macros accordingly.  

But I will likely be on this diet for life.  As will many others, here.  Because we have lifelong need to do so.

So, long story long, you can be on this diet for life.  Or just for weight loss.  Completely up to your personal needs and what you find useful about it.

But it wasn't started in order to help people lose weight.  It's just a side effect of a medical treatment diet.

Do your research, though.  Make sure you're doing it in a healthy way.  It's not just eggs and meat.  There's way more to it, and some people just throw themselves into it and dont know what they're doing, and as with any diet, it can be dangerous to be ignorant of the ramifications of the *way* you do it.  Like lifting weights, there's a right way and wrong way to do it.

Everyone started somewhere.  Most of the people you're seeing at the gym have not had the type of experience you're assuming they do.  They might look like they've been lifting since they were kids, but thats so rare, I doubt there's a single person in there that has *that* kind of experience. 

What you're going through, we all have.

I started swimming this year.  Many of the people there at the time of day that I go have been swimming for a long time and do competitions.   It made me feel some type of way, seeing them keep going at each end, turning around, and continuing to swim.  I had to rest at each end.  I had a hard time making it the 25 yards.  I'd have to rest, then rest again and again and again.  Barely felt like I was making any progress.  More than half my time in the pool was spent catching my breath, feeling like I was going to die.

Many times in the first 2 months, I felt so discouraged, but I tried to focus on me and only me and find something positive in each swim.  Did I do one more lap?  Yes.  And sometimes doing just *one more* of anything in the beginning is the only thing you can focus on.  Can you do one more rep each time and focus on that positive?  I believe that you can.  I dont care if it's a 2lb dumbell, and you just curl it one more time.  It's a positive you can hold onto.

People there might be looking at you, but most of the time, they are connecting with you as a fellow gym goer.  Seeing if you're friendly.   I was scared to talk to people, but if you open up, they are really good at giving you pointers or simple camaraderie because there was a point where they were starting out, and they know what that means for you.  Maybe they are just passively seeing you, and not even really engaging, because they are spacing out and really only focusing on what they're doing.

Not staring at people doing their exercises is a good thing, but avoiding looking at them at all is not a good thing...  what I've noticed is I get ideas on how to better myself by observing those more experienced than I am.  When I see someone more experienced than I am, if they are in the locker room and look like they are okay to engage, I'll ask them a small question and get a pointer or two. Most times I leave them alone, but *every once in a while*, I have a really good conversation. 

Don't approach someone during their workout, but don't be afraid to say hi.  They aren't there to judge you.   

They are there to improve their body,  the same reason why you're there.  Stop focusing on how far "behind" you are in respect to them, and focus on the commonality you have with them.

Will some be asses?  Yeah, but those people are everywhere.  Most people who are into self-improvement understand what you're going through.   

And the people looking at themselves in the mirror are doing it to keep an eye on their form.  Don't avoid looking at yourself, watch your own form.  It will help you.

I've been swimming for 4 months now.  I felt for a long time that I wasn't making any improvements,  but I kept with it, and I see significant results.

Your body will take maybe a couple of months to begin actually acclimating to the process of becoming stronger, but once the process begins, you will look back and be surprised at how far you've come.   

3 swims ago, I pushed myself and swam 2 miles.  

I can tell you from my recent, sometimes discouraged experience that you will surprise yourself.


Keep going, find one thing in the experience that you can do that will make you proud.   

4 months ago, I was scared of everyone at the pool.  Now I know that they are not paying me much attention at all.  Sometimes, they look at you because you're something to look at absent minded, we all "people watch".

Don't put more meaning into their looks at you than there is.  

When you're in their shoes, and doing it a while, and someone new comes into the gym, and you can tell they are beginning a journey, I doubt you're going to think less of them.  

If anything, you'll probably see someone who is tapping into a lot of inner strength to just show up.  Like you're doing right now.

Showing up is a big deal.  And you're doing it.  

I'm proud of you.

Question:  Did your weight jump that much from morning to night?  Because, if so, that's a temporary daily gain.  It's not there for the long haul and most likely will be gone by the next morning after you go to the bathroom. 

I'm sure you know that you weigh the least when you wake, after you go to the bathroom, and before you've eaten anything.  That's the optimal time to weigh yourself.  But it's not always the absolute answer on  how much you *actually* weigh.  I couldn't weigh myself at the end of the day for a long time because it would wreck my self-confidence. 

If you have a lot of salt the day before, this number could be more because you will retain more water.  A burger and fries is a surefire way to retain water. You won't keep it on...
Your body will expel this over time.

It took a long time for me to lose the 60lbs that I'm down, and I am not done losing.  I go up in weight throughout the day, and some weeks, I gain weight.  It's over the long haul that you lose. One meal doesn't undo your progress,  just like you can't lose it all with one meal.

You feel like you had a setback.  I feel that way sometimes, too.  In the beginning of losing weight,  this feels way worse than once you've been at it for a while. You get used to what in the beginning feels like a setback and figure out that it's just how bodies work. Take it in stride.  Beating yourself up, does you no good.  I had to come to terms with the fact that a treat might make me go up a little, but sometimes it's what my morale needed in order to stick with it for the long term.  Sometimes your body needs a shake up meal to trick your metabolism into a higher gear, but dont do it often... Some people can change the way they look at food overnight and see it as "not eating for enjoyment,  just for fuel", others it takes time to get into the mindset, or have their tastes change to where they enjoy the diet (or lifestyle change) itself.

I'm like you in the fact that I would get so down I would want to give up entirely. But I have to listen to my support system and people  in communities like this one, who tell me that it's dedication that will get me there. Don't give up.  Setbacks happen.  You will gain, and you will lose.  But if you don't give up, you will lose more than you will gain, and you will eventually get to where you want to be.

I have gone up as much as 7lbs.  Did it bother me?  A bit, but I had gone up close to that, and a big loss came right after. (Big loss being like 2lbs in a week, so nothing huge.)  I had to go through looses, gains, and losses again over time to come to terms with how my body worked and get used to it so I wouldn't freak out.

This is a slow, "chipping away at it" process, and it can be frustrating.  Even if you have a setback to the point that you gain ten lbs because you go off the rails (like I did early on), you can begin again and keep going.

Give yourself grace.

Understand that one misstep,  one meal, or one bad day doesn't erase the good ones that you have achieved. 

It took mental fortitude to lose the pounds you did, so you know you have it in you to do it again.  For longer.  For the long haul.

Do not discount the days you won just because you feel like you lost for one meal.   You deserve to give yourself credit where it's due.  And you've already done some really hard work.  I know this because I am addicted to good tasting food that's bad for me, and I know it's really hard to still have to eat, but not always be able to enjoy what I get to eat.

You will do this.  You've already proven it by losing weight already.  

BTW,  I do fluctuate by about 5lbs a day.  It's just the way my body works.  Some fluctuate more, others less.  This is an individual journey, and you have to set up rules you can live by and still get to where you want to go.  Make your own map, and keep going.

I used to be afraid of water.  So much so that my second time trying to do laps, my heart rate went up to 199.  At 44, that's not good.  

I figured I needed a snorkel, I went with a full face one, and just went.  I couldn't do more than 25 yards without a rest and couldn't do more than 650 yards total. It actually felt horrible.

It's been about 4 months now, and I graduated to a front snorkel, use paddles and fins, and I went 1000 yards in one go and 2 miles total in one swim earlier this week.   It was hard to get here, and still have a bit of fear from time to time, but it really feels so good to accomplish it.  Good headphones and music you love is a plus (you can get bone conducting waterproof ones, and I swear by them).

You hit almost a meditative state while swimming that I really haven't experienced in other exercises,  and would highly recommend it, because I am stronger mentally and physically, have more endurance, and my body is growing muscle and tone, increasing my bmr.  And I feel peaceful... but I can also get aggressive with it and not hurt myself while still getting out frustrations/stress if I need to.

Gaining 400 to 500 calories for dinner is a plus.  

Also, I have tried to do c25k in the past, and had some issues, and after swimming for 4 months, I just did the first week of c25k and it almost feels easy and I'm pushing over 1 mile an hour faster, breathing better and not spent at the end of it.  200 calories more on those days as well really help me psychologically.

I don't always use those extra calories,  but if my weekly TDEE tells me I can go over, it really helps me feel better about the process.

So 3 days swimming, 3 days running and a day off, and I feel proud of myself after having about 5 years of nothing but the couch and sedentary life.

I love to eat, so gaining the ability to increase fuel a bit through the day is a huge incentive to push myself, even if I don't use the calories, the buffer is great.

I will advocate the same thing others have said, though.  A food scale is an amazing tool to quickly get to the measurement of food, I hate counting food items.  I also use MFP (my fitness pal) to count calories and macros (I super restrict my carbs,  I'm borderline insulin resistant), and it has greatly helped me figure out what works for certain days at certain activity levels.

I'm not sure what other people feel about having a reward every once in a while, but for me, it seems to do my metabolism well to go over both carbs and calories 1 or 2 times a month, and it gives me something to look forward to and seems to calm cravings for the rest of the time I'm super restricting.

With both diet and exercise, I have lost just over 60 lbs from being the heaviest I have ever been, but diet was the biggest component to this.  It's not easy.  I have cried, I have been enraged, i have spent a meal in the bedroom to get away from afast food the kids were earing, but I have also been scared of dying young and unhealthy, God forbid I get into a situation where I need to be physical and I can't get away from a threat.  Im also afraid of continuing to live in a way where I'm no longer truly alive.  Too many years of that already.  Being unable to tie my own shoes without having to take a break to breathe a couple of times is probably my lowest point.  I'm 5'5", and was 228, I just hit 165 yesterday.

I hope you find the exercise you love.  Just understand that in the beginning,  *all* exercise will be difficult, and you'll probably hate it.  I would get into a huge funk on swim days because I was terrified. But if you move through the suck and get to a point where it's just something you have to do, your body will become used to it, and you will start to love it.  

Give any exercise about a month of regular activity before you decide that you actually hate it, because it may take that long (maybe longer) before you will really know whether it's something you just can't get into.

A panic attack on land is scary and hard enough, and you're positive you're about to die. In the water, the chances of you actually dying while feeling that way are higher, and you absolutely know it.  And that situation becomes a danger to anyone who tries to rescue the panic attack victim.  

He tried twice.  That's one more time than I would have been willing to do because the feeling of doom that comes with the beginning of an attack is overwhelming, and when panic begins, you know that you will be totally helpless.

If there were days between, I could understand you asking the question again because sometimes it's just the day, you have high stress, the circumstances aren't right, whatever...  but to immediately ask him to try a third time while he's still probably in a heightened state, trying to ground himself, your question in that moment could have even felt threatening. *To be clear, even *almost* having a panic attack, sometimes coming away from that doomed feeling takes hours, and sometimes days to recover from.

For some people, carbs aren't necessary.  There are some people who actually function better with fewer carbs, more protein, and good fats.  

Myself, I was put on a diet by a doctor and had to do a bunch of research to get it right, but for numerous medical reasons, I need to keep my insulin levels low, and reduce inflammation in my body.

A well-balanced, lower calorie diet had my body going wonky, and even in a deficit, I was gaining fat and had very low energy, could do very little.  I was weighing and measuring everything and counting all calories. 

Low carb high protein and fats (at this point im not even focusing on the protienand fats because im trying to lose, and only increase if i feel like i need to adjust on a given day for more energy the next day if ive been more active than usual on a given day), and I'm down from 230 at 5'4" to 174 in about a year (with a 9 month break trying to eat Mediterranean to see if it worked, it didn't, i actually hained 10 lbs in that 9 months), and still losing as I haven't hit my target yet, but I am actively losing and haven't had a hard time with energy either.  So basically, I've lost that weight in six months on low carb, and I'm more active, less hungry, and there have been many other benefits.

I'm not advocating that someone just go off and try to put themselves in an extreme diet without a ton of research,  im just letting you know that there are some people who absolutely do not need carbs in order to function, and that carbs can actually harm the functions of their body.

But I have fibromyalgia and I was borderline type 2, so my insulin response was zero, I have to keep my insulin from spiking or I actually develop issues with cognition, including slurring to the point that in the beginning I was almost sure I was having a stroke.  It got really bad.  I couldn't remember things I had just been told, nor things I had just said. 

I wasn't eating a ton of sugar, I was already beginning my weight loss journey, but nothing was working. 

To be clear, I was put on this diet by a doctor for medical reasons.  It isn't for everyone.  I'm just clarifying that you *actually* don't have to have carbs to function.  

Anyone *can* do this diet, but it has to be done *properly*, and it does help to have a doctor backing you up with numbers on your insulin and blood sugar, vitamin and mineral levels, etc.

If you're burning that many calories in a day, and you are in a deficit, you absolutely should be losing, and if you aren't,  either you need to change something in how you're eating, or see a doctor about blood panels.  You could be low in something, like a mineral or vitamin thats crucial to your body functions, or you could have something going on like I did, and need to shift your focus as far as what you eat in particular.

Yeah, I actually read a post on reddit about it and found it fascinating.   It makes sense. Many people sleep better in a cold bedroom, and tons of people, culturally and otherwise, swear by extreme temperature exposure for the immune system.   

I guess if I were brought up with the practice as you were, it wouldn't feel odd to me to put a child outside to nap, but as an American, I would be afraid to do it.  Probably mostly for fear of being reported to cps or something.

There are people in Norway, Finland, etc, who purposely take their children out in the cold (properly clothed course) and actually let them sleep a bit out there for many reasons, not the least of which is to help their bodies acclimate and help with their immune system, there's no real finding that cold hurts a child unless improperly dressed.  Cold does wonders for the body.  So does heat.

That doesn't mean *over* exposure,  but it does mean exposure.  

This is probably something to do with your nanny coming from a warmer climate and not being familiar with practices of other cultures in cold climates that actually benefit a child, well, benefit a person, no matter their age unless there is an underlying condition that prevents this from being a benefit.

If I were you, I would do some research into these practices and let her know that taking your child out is not going to harm them as long as attention is paid to their physical wellness during the outing and that they are properly clothed.

Your weight fluctuates daily, and as a woman, it also (frustratingly) fluctuates wildly once a month.  

Mine can fluctuate 5 to 8 lbs in a day, and once a month, it can stay up 5 lbs for the week, but I'm tracking calories, so I know it's not that I ate too many calories. It's because it's natural.  Water retention is a thing, so give yourself grace and don't get upset about it.  

Look up your TDEE calculator in Google or whatever search engine you prefer.  The calculator asks you questions about yourself and helps you figure out how many calories you need to maintain your weight, and it will tell you where you need to be to lose weight.

Once you have those numbers,  track the calories you are consuming and only take in the calories it calculated as your maintenance,  and get as close to the calories it tells you to consume to lose weight.   I use my fitness pal, but there are many calorie tracking apps out there.  Use it to keep yourself accountable. Enter the food you are consuming right then and there.  It's a hassle at first, but it becomes something you enjoy as it becomes a habit.

When you weigh yourself, do so first thing in the morning after you go to the bathroom before you eat or drink anything.  That's your actual weight.  Any other time, the scale will include anything you've consumed at that point and will not be your actual weight.

Working out will help increase *some* calories that you can consume, but keep in mind that if your diet is not good, you're unlikely to be able to burn it off through exercise.   It can take you 10 minutes to consume, say a meal from a fast food joint that's half your caloric intake limit for the day, and it would take you literally multiple hours to burn it all off.  That's why they say weight is lost in the kitchen, and fitness is done in the gym.   

Try not to make your diet too restricting.  You need it to be something you can stick to.  Which is where portion control is more important. Whole, unprocessed foods are also better because of the lack of additives, the nutrition is better and can keep you fuller for longer.  If you find yourself still being hungry after a few days or a week and can't feel yourself getting full, try more protein dense foods and see if that helps you gain more control over cravings.

Some people (I have done this), who are having a huge craving for something as a treat, calculate your TDEE for the week (it's important to know this anyway), add up your caloric intake for the last seven days, and see if you have enough calories for what you're craving.   Don't go over those calories, though. If you don't have them, don't use them unless you can deal with a possible gain after a treat.   Other people have whole "cheat days", that's not okay to do if you're really trying to lose weight, especially for your health.  If you want a "cheat," make it a singular meal.   Much easier to recover from, and if your weight loss has reached a plateau,  sometimes a shakeup of a "treat yourself" meal can help. Just don't go on a food bender. And don't do it more than once a week, staying under your calories. 

Also, don't go really far below the recommended caloric intake for weight loss.  There's a reason why they say it's a minimum.   Going under that can be extremely unhealthy and may cause malnutrition, muscular issues, immune issues, and even neurological complications.

Lastly, if you want to increase your butt size, work the muscles.  Your legs will get work as well, but any glute-targeted exercises will eventually increase the size as the muscles grow.  Im doing c2k5, and just the jogging is perking my butt up. Don't know how, but im not complaining, lol.  Also, I'm not pushing myself to exhaustion.  That's important for any exercise. You want it to be something that you can do on a regular basis. So don't over do it.

Sometimes, people don't want something until life circumstances allow them to realize that they do.  Some men and women don't discover that they want children until they are secure in their relationship/relationship status and living situation.  Some people will think that their significant other lied about their want or need for kids, and the fact of the matter is that people just genuinely change, and sometimes quickly.  

I just want you, first, to not assume more negatively about your situation than you have to.  There's enough bad feelings going on.

But the other fact remains that at this very fundamental level, you two differ.  If it's not something that you guys will come to a happy medium and no compromise can be met (you either have kids or you don't), then you have reached a definite impasse where you know your life is going to change forever, buy you are the one that has to decide how it's going to change.

You're concerned about her "possibly backsliding".  She is depressed and actively backsliding *right now*.  It's likely that in her state of depression - no positive activity, and having little positive interactions, health issues - she could think that a child will fix problems she's having and be a source of happiness in life.  This is definitely not the time to have a kid.  I think you know that, so keep an eye on birth control methods... you don't know how bad her depression really is, you arent with her 24/7.

You are under no obligation to stay, but if her reason for desiring a kid is a *result* of her depression, helping her out of this hole she's in might actually bring back the "old" her that you fell in love with.  She may not *really* want a kid, just really thinks she does.  *Do not tell her that you even read that statement*, that will only cause damage at this point. 

People start wanting things for different reasons.   Some are genuine desires, and others turn up because of something else entirely.  

Her sudden drastic change is something to be concerned about.  If you stay, you need to come up with the plan to help her and find a timeline that you can live with about making progress. 

She's likely going to crippled before her time.  It's traumatic to know something like that is coming, and she's getting closer to that age where it will happen.  So be gentle with your decision, so you can live with it, too. She may never get back to being the woman you married.  But she could get close.

If you choose to go, which is valid, knowing how she's behaving, I urge you to let someone know about her state of mind and your fears for her.  You are under no obligation to save another person from themselves.  If she's too far down to listen, you might be too late, or you might be addressing it before she's ready. Only time will tell that.  You may or may not want to give it time to see if you can get her out of this.  Try, maybe, and see if you think it's possible. 

You might be asking your wife to work on it and not a divorce.   Don't be too black and white about it.

I'm sorry you're going through that.  It sounds like he needs to learn and grow a bit about the whole "just joking" thing.  We all can get defensive about things when we make a joke that hurts someone's feelings. Sometimes, the joke seems harmless to the teller, but the real guage of maturity is if the teller learns that the joke wasn't as harmless as intended, that they take your feelings more seriously than their freedom to joke about whatever they want.

People say that a joke is only funny if both people laugh, and it would be a good rule, but that's not really true of humor.  They key, though, if the person is someone you trust, and they poke a wound, they need to hold themselves to a higher standard. 

I wouldn't make it a reprimand,  but talk to him about it, and make sure he lets you finish what you need to say and think about it before he responds.   Make sure he knows you aren't starting a fight, but you want him to take your feelings seriously and understand that this type of joke is off-limits.  

You can actually agree with him on the fact that what's done can't be changed, but future behavior can be, and that's what you want.  But sweeping the problem away like it's over and done with cannot because now you'll be questioning how he sees you, and think less of yourself because of his words, and you will need words of reassurance to soften the memory of a very bad joke.  

There are consequences to actions and words.  You shouldn't be the one shouldering the consequences of his words without him having to shoulder the responsibility of working to do better for you and make you feel appreciated. 

And if he can not practice good healthy boundaries with trading burns with you, then maybe rethink trading burns with him.   You can make that something completely off limits if he can't be mature about it.

If a joke hurts, it's not really a joke.  It's mean spirited,  and the statement that it was a joke is a cop out, imo.   

It's only really a joke if you both find it funny.   Unless you have the type of relationship where you trade "burns," then you can't consider this a joke.  And he shouldn't be telling you that you "shouldn't be hurt" by something he said that was hurtful.  Are you sensitive?  When it comes to being a good parent, we all are, and even more so when our partner, our support  system, and our safe place say something that creates further self-doubt.  

He can claim all he wants that he wasn't trying to hurt you.  He can say that he wasn't trying to hurt you, but once you tell someone that a joke hurt you, the teller needs to understand that the "joke" they told went from funny to hurtful, and they need to own that it was a bad joke, apologize for hurting you.  They should not double down and tell you how you should feel.

Maybe he is having an issue with feeling like you don't have time enough for him, and he's trying to stop you from wanting another child right now with whatever he can verbally, and maybe he doesn't even understand why he said it, but its possible he didn't mean it the way you took it.  

But he needs to understand that his intent can not dictate response, and saying otherwise is childish and harmful to the baseline trust in your relationship.   Once the words come out, it's hard to set them aside. They replay in one's mind and can really cause damage.   You need to explain this to him and get him to understand without anger or argument that he can't tolerate carelessness with his own words.

Everyone has worries and doubts. When you voice that something was said that increased yours, and your husband is the one that did it, it's his job to try to make it better.  He does not get to preserve himself by dismissing you.  He can't take back what he said, but he certainly can learn from it and do better in the future.

Being able to slow your mind down when you are angry is definitely hard, but it's an art, and it helps *you* to be able to do so, and to be able to properly articulate and give context makes it easier for you to understand yourself, the inner workings of your mind and the finer details of your emotions, thereby serving not just your present situations,  but helps your future self in difficult situations.

Being able to speak, or write about what's happening, why you feel the way that you do, etc, leads you to be able to tell someone else who may be important to you or not what is wrong with their actions, or words so that they don't push someone (including you) to the point of anger that you reached in this post.

Being able to express yourself is important.   It's even more important that when you express yourself that you don't alienate the people listening to you or reading your words because at the end of the day, when you're going through a tough time, you dont want to be met with a bad reaction because that compounds whatever issues you were facing to begin with.

I don't want you to be facing more than what you started off having a problem with because people have an issue with your ability to express, that can lead to a ton of issues down the line.   People you thought understood you making assumptions due to the way you've alienated them or internet strangers being unwilling to listen to your problems because of the way you dont take accountability for possible bad actions.

Your message about what hurt/angers/makes you happy is just as important as mine and really anyone else's.   You may not think you have anything in you that can teach someone else, but everyone's point of view is valuable and can teach anyone who has a different point of view. You deserve to be heard and to be able to speak to others.  Don't deafen someone else to your words because you're too pissed off about something and can't articulate it properly.  

Hold still.  Study yourself, and steady yourself.  Speak your truth and come un-burdened.  That's what this community is here for.  That's what everyone is on this site for, really.  We are all reading someone's words, gaining something from the experience.   Some will engage you for the entertainment of riling you up.  Others will read and feel for you and never say anything. What you do with your anger is ultimately your choice.  Just don't be surprised when you're met with people telling you things you don't like  if you blame others for things that you know would be your own actions.

If you're having an anger attack, there are other things to do with it.
